data.title: Trump Media’s investors lost $2.2 billion while president holds $460 million stake
data.description: By the time Ske Jarzenske cast a third straight ballot for Donald Trump, he had something extra riding on the outcome: his brokerage account. The 52-year-old resident of Austin, Texas, had poured 20% of his net worth into Trump Media & Technology Group, convinced that a second Trump presidency would make him money. Now, Jarzenske’s investment is down 88.5%, according to a Charles Schwab statement ​he showed Reuters on the condition that the dollar amount not be published. He’s one of the buyers who, along with the rest of the firm’s outside investors, have collectively absorbed more than $2.2 billion in losses, according to a Reuters estimate. “It’s been very disappointing and ‌difficult to watch,” said Jarzenske. Trump Media shares collapsed as the company’s social media business burned through cash while struggling to attract new clients — and its investments in cryptocurrencies fell sharply in value. Even hardcore boosters of the stock told Reuters they are losing hope as shares hit record lows. The Reuters estimate of investor losses is based on the performance of shares sold into the market by Trump Media, its predecessor entities, including Digital World Acquisition Corp. and Trump Media & Technology Group, as well as insiders such as the founders and management. The figure is also adjusted to account for share buybacks and based on company filings and court records detailing share issuances and sales. Trump Media filings show dozens of equity transactions since 2021, ​which generated $2.7 billion. Reuters calculated losses or gains for each tranche depending on whether the shares currently trade above or below their issue price. Total losses were reduced to adjust for the impact of share buybacks. In response to a detailed ⁠list of questions from Reuters, Trump Media said in an emailed statement: “TMTG has built a strong balance sheet and is focused on creating value for shareholders, including its proposed merger with TAE Technologies.” TAE Technologies is a nuclear fusion energy firm. The company also vigorously disputed Reuters methodology, saying, “Your dubious, biased calculations misrepresent the facts, ​market dynamics, and TMTG’s public filings.” The company declined to specify flaws in Reuters calculations but its general counsel, Scott Glabe, said in a letter to Reuters that “millions of shares of Trump Media change hands in the public markets every trading day, and information about whether any given seller achieved a profit or loss is unknowable.” The Reuters methodology is consistent with the mark-to-market accounting practices fund managers are required to ​use when calculating their performance, in line with the long-running Reuters practice for assessing investor losses or gains on shares and was reviewed by three finance professors who said it was the generally accepted way to assess investor gains and losses. Cashing in Unlike ​any other president before him, Trump and his family have sought to monetize political loyalty, invoking Make America Great Again (MAGA) adherence in investment pitches involving equities and crypto ventures. He has lent his name to a social media company, a meme coin and cryptocurrency tokens. Investors in four major Trump-backed crypto projects–including the president’s meme coin, the Trump family’s crypto exchange, World Liberty Financial, its bitcoin mining operation, American Bitcoin, and a blockchain company, AI Financial-lost a combined $2.3 billion through April, as the value of their digital tokens crashed, Reuters reported earlier. Trump Media’s shareholders now face a similar reckoning. Some are standing by the president. Others wonder whether the movement they backed with their votes and their savings has left them behind. Losses continued as the president’s approval ratings hit all-time lows ​and Democrats won control of the House and Senate on Tuesday. Most Americans believe Trump’s business interests, which include his crypto projects and real estate ventures, influenced his decisions as president since he returned to power, a Reuters/Ipsos opinion poll found. Almost half of the Republicans surveyed held that view, along with 69% of independents. The White House ​responded to a detailed list of questions about the story by referring Reuters to Trump Media. As with many of the recent Trump-backed property deals and the four main crypto ventures backed by the first family–the Trump meme coin, World Liberty Financial, American Bitcoin and AI Financial–the Trumps invested little to none of their own money into Trump Media, securities filings ‌show. Even as retail ⁠investors lose money, President Trump’s 114.75 million shares of the company, which he received without paying any cash in 2024 as a part of Trump Media’s merger with a special purpose acquisition company called Digital World Acquisition, are still worth about $460 million at the Thursday closing price of $4.02 per share. Trump’s stake had a paper value of more than $6 billion when the stock was trading near its high. Shareholder Jarzenske said he still supports the president, but wishes the family would do more for investors. He feels it’s unfair insiders have made such handsome gains. “The Trump family, they say they care but to me they have all this money and they keep making more money, but how about the little people?” said Jarzenske. Trump Media did not respond to questions about Jarzenske’s assertions. Crypto is an inherently risky investment, due in part to its volatility and a general lack of regulatory oversight. Trump Media also discloses a long list of risks to investors in regulatory filings, including that the value of the brand ​may diminish if Trump’s popularity were to suffer. ‘As rigged as the elections’ Reuters interviewed more than a dozen Trump Media shareholders, all of ⁠them three-time Trump voters except for one, who is a Canadian resident. They said their experience with the stock had left them reeling. They include a trucker in Washington state, a retired police officer in Oklahoma, and a flooring company worker in Michigan. Like Jarzenske, all the shareholders said they once believed that Truth Social would become one of the world’s dominant media and streaming platforms. Hugh Baron, a 63-year old California retiree and former small business owner and Trader Joe’s worker, said he bought ​more than 1,000 shares, some as high as $53.54. He said his holdings are down 88.5%. “The markets are as rigged as the elections,” Baron said. Claims of widespread election fraud are false, as courts and election officials have consistently rejected them. Patricia ​Spoerl, 64, a nurse in Colorado, said she ⁠bought shares at an average of $45.32, believing they would triple in price and help underwrite her retirement. She is now sitting on a “painful” loss of about $28,000. “I’m really sad and disappointed,” said Spoerl. “I always knew it would be a risk but I expected when Trump became president he’d have more clout to check into the SEC and figure out why this stock is being held back.” Spoerl and Baron, like the other investors interviewed by Reuters, believe that Trump Media has been the victim of mismanagement and “naked short selling,” where institutional traders sell shares short without first borrowing them in hopes the price will fall, allowing them to buy back the shares at a lower price. Reuters was not able to ⁠find evidence of naked ​short selling in Trump Media shares. Current short interest in the company — often used as a gauge of investor sentiment — is at a level that analysts consider below average for companies of ​a similar size. The company’s social media business has yet to take off. Trump Media’s revenue has been flat at around $4 million a year for the past three years. Its timing on becoming a crypto treasury — or a company that holds crypto as a main reserve asset — was poor because its bitcoin purchase, announced by the company, came near its peak before a steep crash in price. The company spent ​more than $200 million building the Truth Social streaming service, which generated just $630,000 in revenues between its launch in August 2024 and the end of June 2026, regulatory filings show. Since the midterm elections, seen as a rebuke of Trump’s policies, shares have fallen 32%.

data.title: The U.S. added 165,000 jobs in October, a bright spot for the economy
data.description: The U.S. economy added 165,000 jobs in October, in a surprise that far outpaced expectations by economists and analysts. The unemployment rate in October dropped to 4.1%, extending a near historically-low streak. “Through September 2026, the US labor market had kept unemployment below 5% for 61 straight months,” wrote Apollo Global Management chief economist Torsten Slok on Friday. He noted that the labor market was “on the verge of becoming the longest period of sustained labor market strength in modern US history.” While that steady figure reflects fulsome employment across the nation, economists also say that it reflects a stagnation. “The problem is the low rate of turnover,” said Diane Swonk, chief economist at KPMG, also noting that “fewer people are entering the labor force.” But the data showed that sluggish wage growth did not meaningfully improve. Average hourly earnings rose 3.1% from a year ago, which was also more than expected, but that continues to track well below the rate of inflation, as it has since March. Inflation is 3.7% and on the upswing, as of the most recent Consumer Price Index released on Oct. 14. Business inflation is rising even faster, a likely sign of what’s to come for consumers at grocery stores and retail outlets.

data.title: Tesla to wind down Cybertruck production after years of poor sales in few markets
data.description: Tesla will wind down Cybertruck production at its Texas gigafactory around mid-2027, CEO Elon Musk said on Friday, after years of persistently weak sales for a futuristic model once touted as a rival to legacy pickup trucks that ultimately only sold in just a handful of markets because of its heavy, angular design. Musk said in an X post the production wind-down would enable the automaker to accommodate increased output of its newly launched Cybercab model, which the billionaire has made central to Tesla's robotaxi ambitions. While it was not immediately clear whether Cybertruck production would be moved to another facility or phased out entirely, the automaker's Austin plant is the only known Tesla facility equipped to manufacture the model's specialized components. In response to a user on X, Musk called the Cybertruck the "best vehicle Tesla has ever made" and the wind-down the "end of an era." Tesla did not immediately respond to a Reuters request for comment sent outside regular business hours. The US EV maker only began delivering the Cybertruck to customers in late 2023. According to Kelley Blue Book, the company only sold 20,237 Cybertrucks in the US last year, down 48% from 38,965 in 2024. Before the pickup truck launched, Musk had predicted annual sales of 250,000 units. "It doesn't make sense to keep it going when it's not meeting its targets," said former Aston Martin CEO Andy Palmer. "Every rational auto guy would say the same." "It will no doubt only be a rounding error on Tesla's balance sheet, but the statistics speak for themselves." Right from its unveiling in 2019, the Cybertruck was a controversial choice for Musk. Its angular design was mocked by pickup truck purists and safety experts predicted it would be hard to gain approval for sale in key markets like Europe. The unveiling event itself was marred when Musk tried to prove that its windows were shatterproof by having metal balls thrown at them - only to leave massive cracks in two of them. During Cybertruck's official launch in 2023, Musk touted it as a futuristic competitor to pickup trucks from General Motors and Ford, saying "finally, the future will look like the future." But the vehicle has struggled to meet those expectations. Automotive analyst Automotive analyst Felipe Munoz said that although the Cybertruck has been called a failure because of its poor sales, electric pick-ups from Ford and others have also flopped in the US market. "All of them lost the competition because electric pick ups aren't popular in the US," Munoz said. But Cybertruck's sharp-edged stainless-steel design limited its prospects in markets like Europe where EVs are more popular. Regulatory approval was impossible for Europe because of rules there concerning pedestrian impact. "Anywhere where you have crash regulation that takes into account pedestrian impact, that Cybertruck won't go, can't go," former Aston Martin CEO Palmer said. The Cybercab, which has butterfly doors and no steering wheel, pedals or mirrors, is one of Musk's key bets in his push to turn Tesla into an AI and robotics company rather than just an automaker. Musk has said he sees it as Tesla's main autonomous model supplying a global network of robotaxis. After years of delays to Musk's self-driving targets, Tesla began offering paid rides in a small fleet of Cybercabs in Austin in September. However, the automaker still has to answer the US auto safety agency's questions on whether it has properly self-certified Cybercab to demonstrate compliance with federal motor vehicle safety standards. "Cybertruck was an incredible technology development platform and lives on through Cybercab," Cybertruck lead engineer Wes Morrill said on X.

data.title: Global market rout deepens after midterms intensify AI fears
data.description: HONG KONG — An intensifying rout of tech stocks hit global markets Friday, with a surge of red tickers spreading from Wall Street to Asia and Europe after the blue wave of the U.S. midterm elections fueled fears over AI development. The steep losses in Asia — Japan’s Nikkei suffered its worst week since 2020 — came after a dramatic plunge in U.S. tech stocks following the success of anti-AI candidates, which deepened concerns about the durability of the AI boom. Some $2.3 billion in market value was wiped off the tech-focused Nasdaq 100, which dropped 6.3% on Thursday. Another $2.8 trillion was erased from the S&P 500’s market value as it fell 4.4% — their worst day in 18 months, when President Donald Trump’s global tariffs rocked markets. U.S. futures were mixed early Friday, but European shares also opened lower after the dramatic selloff continued in Asia. South Korea’s Kospi index tumbled more than 8%, triggering a temporary market-wide trading halt. There, AI data center memory suppliers Samsung and SK Hynix plunged more than 10% in the early hours, before recovering some of their losses. Japan’s Nikkei 225 index fell as much as 6%, entering bear-market territory. In Taiwan, home to some of the most critical AI companies, including chip supplier TSMC, the benchmark TAIEX index dropped 9%. London’s FTSE 100 index fell by 1.6% on Friday open, while the French and German indices, CAC40 and DAX, took similar hits. “Markets are being punished according to their dependence on the U.S. AI infrastructure cycle,” Charu Chanana, Chief Investment Strategist at Singapore-based SAXO Markets, told NBC News in emailed comments. The companies in Taiwan, South Korea and Japan are “clearly highly linked to the global AI capex cycle and hence I am not surprised to see the magnitude of correction today following the sharp correction in the U.S.,” Tai Hui, J.P. Morgan’s APAC Chief Market Strategist, told NBC News in emailed comments. The plunge came after the stunning midterm results that will see the rise of a crop of anti-AI and anti-data center politicians, including Gov.-elect Gina Hinojosa in Texas, the largest data center market in the country. A Democratic Congress could tighten scrutiny of the industry, including AI infrastructure projects, which could cause delays and additional costs, adding to worries investors have about the profitability of these investments. Recent months have been nothing short of a rollercoaster for Asian investors, who saw their paper fortunes grow by magnitudes in June during the AI stock boom, but have been suffering from a brutal recent sell-off.

data.title: Salon, an early staple of internet discourse, announces it will shut down
data.description: WASHINGTON — Salon, one of the early internet's most influential websites that featured sharp voices and political and cultural journalism backed by a liberal sensibility, announced Thursday it would shut down after 31 years of publication. “It has been an extraordinary privilege,” the outlet said in a farewell note. The announcement, seen as a surprise, cited the fact that “the business realities of independent digital journalism have changed profoundly over the years.” It did not immediately indicate what would become of its employees, though some reported they had lost their jobs. “Over three decades, Salon has brought together politics, culture, criticism and ideas in a way that was distinctly our own,” the unsigned farewell note said. “Our journalism examined power and politics, questioned assumptions, surfaced stories that deserved attention and made room for perspectives that were too often overlooked. Our writers and editors helped shape conversations about the forces changing our lives.” It began shortly after the internet went big Salon began its life in the mid-1990s, barely three years after the internet itself went mainstream and a time when the “World Wide Web” was still written out in that fashion. It launched a decade before the newspaper and print magazine markets imploded — and a decade, too, before the rise of social media fragmented the journalism world. As its name suggested, Salon was initially styled as an online magazine and meeting place, a site where more provocative opinions and stories that might not be at home in daily newspapers or even then-dominant newsweeklies like Time or Newsweek could surface and generate discussion. It quickly became a place where writers wanted their work to appear. “The timing was right — readers were tired of bland, market-tested media products, and the internet allowed us to launch something original, something with a strong voice,” founder David Talbot said on the outlet’s five-year anniversary in 2000. It drew a cadre of high-profile writers and people who would become famous, including Jake Tapper and Glenn Greenwald. Two of its editors-in-chief, Talbot and Joan Walsh, went on to become prominent progressive political voices as well. As the internet grew, so did Salon's competition. Slate emerged the following year, and soon after, online magazines became the order of the day. Eventually, older print publications like The Atlantic began putting more content online and the marketplace of online ideas grew. Salon used Princess Diana's death in 1997 to go beyond its culture-and-criticism roots and wade into breaking-news coverage. No word on what becomes of its content Salon did not immediately say what would become of its immense online archives, which include three decades of stories from across the world and across topics and genres. In the statement, Salon also made a point of thanking its readers. “You came to Salon for the journalism, the dialogue, the essays, the criticism, the unexpected discoveries and the sense that there was a place on the internet where ideas mattered,” it said. “You read, shared, challenged, subscribed, wrote to us and kept coming back. Your engagement made Salon a publication and a community, and it gave our work meaning. We are so grateful for the time you spent with us.”

data.title: Holiday hiring and AI in focus with October jobs report on deck
data.description: A lukewarm job market may have gained some steam last month, as companies began hiring workers for the holiday season, although slowing wage growth and the impact of AI remain big concerns. The Bureau of Labor Statistics is set to release the October jobs report at 8:30 a.m. ET on Friday. Economists expect the report to show the U.S. added 59,000 roles, up from September’s 29,000, according to a survey conducted by Dow Jones. The unemployment rate is projected to remain unchanged at 4.2% Workers’ wages, however, are expected to show annual growth of 2.9%, well below the latest rate of inflation. In September, the annual rate of inflation rose to 3.7%. Since March, wages have grown more slowly than the pace of prices. While publicly traded tech giants have boomed — Thursday’s massive selloff aside — workers are seeing little payoff, all while remaining on edge to see what the technology will do to their jobs. Those companies, which are pouring hundreds of billions of dollars into developing artificial intelligence and data centers, are also driving up prices across the economy for consumers, from Apple products to Nintendo Switch 2 game consoles to laptop computers. As voters turned up at ballot boxes around the country on Tuesday, 75% of them told NBC News’ exit poll that the state of the economy was “not so good or poor.” Voters also ranked the economy as their number one issue when casting their ballots. The war with Iran remains a stalemate, which is also driving up energy prices, as is the Ukraine-Russia war. At the same time, the labor market is sluggish. On a broad basis, job growth this year has significantly lagged the last few years. At a total of 612,000 jobs added through September, it surpasses 2025’s near-zero growth, but pales in comparison to the millions of jobs added each year from 2020 through 2024. “The problem is the low rate of turnover,” said Diane Swonk, chief economist at KPMG, also noting that “fewer people are entering the labor force.” The unemployment rate has remained historically low for an extended period of time, but workers who want or need to change jobs have few options. The wars and the AI boom may be supporting some employment creation, however. “Recent [third quarter] GDP data showed extremely strong business investment,” said Bank of America’s Shruti Mishra. She said that she expects to see some payoff on Friday from the unprecedented tech spending, which could “continue to support employment in construction and manufacturing, both through the data-center buildout and production of AI-related equipment.” Some see the benefits of AI showing up in recent jobs data due to the construction of data centers. The BLS reported that manufacturing jobs increased by 9,000 in September, and are up 72,000 from “since a recent low in December 2025.” Construction jobs grew 11,000 last month, at a steady rate of “an average of 10,000 jobs per month over the prior 12 months,” BLS said. But, the AI boom is facing rising risks: from Democrats who have pledged data center pauses or bans sweeping Tuesday’s elections, to interest rates that remain highly elevated compared to recent years. On Thursday, the S&P 500 and Nasdaq Composite suffered their worst one-day selloffs since April 2025, in the wake of the Democratic rout. The Nasdaq 100, which includes heavyweights such as Tesla and Microsoft, plummeted 6%, erasing more than $2 trillion in value. “Some sectors, like residential construction and parts of manufacturing, may be sensitive to higher rates and tighter financial conditions. If financial conditions continue to tighten, demand for labor may soften more broadly,” Citi economist Veronica Clark wrote earlier this week. “Of course, there is also the possibility that productivity gains (perceived or real) from AI adoption could weigh on hiring, or also that the cost of adopting AI could mean less funds to hire workers,” Clark added. One bright spot in Friday’s report could be hiring for the upcoming holiday season. In October, the Indeed Hiring Lab reported that “seasonal hiring is off to its best start in several years.” “That early strength is one reason to expect the momentum could carry past this year’s holiday shopping season,” the firm said. “A group of large employers is posting far fewer seasonal jobs than they did a year ago, but making up for some of that drop by shifting toward hiring more non-seasonal, part-time roles — a potential sign of optimism heading into the final months of 2026.” There are other factors at play, too. Andy Challenger, workplace expert at outplacement firm Challenger, Gray and Christmas said “tariffs continue to work through supply chains, and retailers are leaning on automation, existing associates, and on-demand pools before hiring net-new seasonal workers.”

data.title: LIV Golf is headed toward bankruptcy barring a last-minute rescue
data.description: LIV Golf, the breakaway golf tour backed by Saudi royalty and some of the biggest names in the game, indicated Thursday it planned for bankruptcy — a stunning conclusion to an effort that had received billions of dollars in backing. Documents filed in New Jersey Bankruptcy Court showed LIV plans to file for Chapter 11 bankruptcy protection as it seeks relief from creditors. It was not immediately clear how much it owed. Saudi Arabia’s Public Investment Fund has invested more than $5 billion in the company since 2022. Formed in 2021 by a group of golfers led by Phil Mickleson and Greg Norman who expressed dissatisfaction with the long-running PGA Tour, LIV attracted numerous bold-faced names including Jon Rahm, Bryson DeChambeau and Dustin Johnson with millions in guaranteed payouts. Its creation set off a quasi-civil war of sorts in the game between LIV players and others committed to sticking with the PGA, whose tournaments were seen as more competitive. By contrast, LIV’s events were accused of lacking drama because players’ payouts were guaranteed. While LIV tournaments attracted healthy audiences overseas, they failed to land a long-term TV partner in the U.S., crippling its visibility and revenue streams. Multiple outlets reported earlier this week that LIV had sought a last-minute investment with a large private equity group, only to see the deal fall apart. Sports media outlet The Athletic reported the group, BC Partners, did not receive enough commitments from golfers interested in reviving the tour, which had seen multiple events canceled this year, including a team championship.

data.title: Tech stocks plunge on worries about AI and Democrats’ midterm landslide
data.description: Shares in technology companies dropped sharply Thursday, compounding recent declines that have sparked concerns about the durability of the artificial intelligence boom that has driven much of recent U.S. economic growth. The tech-focused Nasdaq 100 index dropped 5% in mid-morning trading, to its lowest level in five months. The broader Nasdaq Composite, which tracks more than just tech stocks, also entered “correction” on Thursday, which is when a stock or index declines at least 10%. Tech stocks have surged in recent years as excitement about artificial intelligence has fueled billions of dollars in investments in, and by, the companies that make chips and infrastructure necessary for its development and operation. Since Election Day 2024, the Nasdaq has surged almost 40%. But questions about whether AI will enable the kind of productivity necessary to generate returns on those investments have grown louder in recent months. Also contributing to losses were the commanding Democratic victories across the country in Tuesday’s midterm elections. Numerous Democrats who won races for governor, attorney general, Senate and House seats have pledged to slow or halt the construction of AI data centers. Texas, Ohio, Michigan and Georgia were of particular concern, because they are all large data center markets. Elon Musk’s companies, SpaceX and Tesla, each slid around 10%, largely in response to the midterm results. Musk, the world’s first trillionaire, donated hundreds of millions to help elect Republican midterm candidates. Until Tuesday’s rout, he was seen as one of the largest potential beneficiaries of Republican victories. Now that voters have so resoundingly rejected the GOP, Musk and his companies face the prospect of tighter regulation and even potential investigations at both the state and federal levels. The sell-off was triggered by two lackluster earnings reports from major chipmakers, Qualcomm and Arm Holdings, which were released on Wednesday night. Both companies posted results that investors generally viewed as mixed. In early trading, the two companies led the Nasdaq indexes lower. Qualcomm tumbled 9% while Arm Holdings slipped around 15%. Earnings reports like these have rattled investors in recent months because of the hundreds of billions of dollars that are being poured into the AI sector. The S&P 500 also fell nearly 3%, with memory and chip firms SanDisk, Western Digital, AMD, Seagate and Micron all plunging around 10%. The Dow Jones Industrial Average dropped nearly 700 points. The biggest contributor to the Dow’s drop was Nvidia, which sold-off by 7%, its largest one-day decline since April 2025. Nvidia is the most important supplier to any AI firm, but as investors raise questions about returns, the euphoria in the industry is fading. Nvidia’s shares have tanked 15% over the past three months. Dow components Cisco and Caterpillar, which are both major suppliers to AI data centers, also dropped around 5%.
